flawed_step: Step 5: independence of N(v) does not imply that its vertices use at most two colors in a proper 3-coloring.
counterexample: Let H have vertices 0,...,11 and edges {01,04,06,09,12,15,17,23,26,28,34,37,39,45,48,5-10,5-11,6-10,6-11,7-8,7-11,8-10,9-10,9-11}. This is a triangle-free 4-regular graph with no proper 3-coloring.
assessment_summary:
Proof attempt and audit:
1. [JUSTIFIED] Assume the statement is false and choose a counterexample G with the fewest vertices; this is a valid minimal-counterexample setup.
2. [JUSTIFIED] G is connected: otherwise every smaller component is 3-colorable by minimality, and their colorings combine into a 3-coloring of G.
3. [JUSTIFIED] Every vertex of G has degree at least 3: if deg(v)≤2, minimality gives a 3-coloring of G−v, and some color unused by the at most two neighbors of v extends it to G.
4. [JUSTIFIED] For every vertex v, N(v) is independent, since an edge between two neighbors of v would form a triangle.
5. [NOT JUSTIFIED] Claim that, because N(v) is independent and has at most four vertices, its vertices use at most two colors in every 3-coloring of G−v. Independence imposes no equality between their colors, so three independent neighbors may receive all three colors. This is the first failure.
6. [NOT JUSTIFIED AS A DEDUCTION] If the neighbors used at most two colors, the coloring would indeed extend to v, but Step 5 has not established that premise.
7. [NOT JUSTIFIED] The claimed contradiction and universal 3-colorability conclusion therefore do not follow.
8. [JUSTIFIED] Define H by the edge set in counterexample. Its neighborhoods are N(0)={1,4,6,9}, N(1)={0,2,5,7}, N(2)={1,3,6,8}, N(3)={2,4,7,9}, N(4)={0,3,5,8}, N(5)={1,4,10,11}, N(6)={0,2,10,11}, N(7)={1,3,8,11}, N(8)={2,4,7,10}, N(9)={0,3,10,11}, N(10)={5,6,8,9}, and N(11)={5,6,7,9}.
9. [JUSTIFIED] Every displayed neighborhood has four vertices, so H is 4-regular and hence has maximum degree 4.
10. [JUSTIFIED] Comparing each displayed neighborhood with the edge set shows that no two vertices in any N(v) are adjacent; therefore H contains no triangle.
11. [JUSTIFIED] To test 3-colorability, suppose H has a proper coloring c with colors A,B,C.
12. [JUSTIFIED] Vertices 0,1,2,3,4 induce the 5-cycle 0-1-2-3-4-0. Any proper 3-coloring of this cycle has color multiplicities 2,2,1. If s is the vertex with the uniquely occurring color, then after renaming A,B,C, cyclically c_s,c_{s+1},c_{s+2},c_{s+3},c_{s+4}=C,A,B,A,B.
13. [JUSTIFIED] The five possible values of s are exhaustive, and each is impossible: s=0 gives (c0,...,c4)=(C,A,B,A,B), forcing c5=C,c6=A,c9=B, so vertex 10 sees all three colors; s=1 gives (B,C,A,B,A), forcing c5=B,c6=C,c7=A, so vertex 11 sees all three; s=2 gives (A,B,C,A,B), with c5∈{A,C},c6=B,c7=C,c8=A,c9∈{B,C}; colorability of vertex 10 forces c5=A and c9=B, after which vertex 11 sees A,B,C; s=3 gives (B,A,B,C,A), with c5∈{B,C},c6∈{A,C},c7=B,c8=C,c9=A; colorability of vertex 10 forces c5=C, after which vertex 11 sees C,B,A; s=4 gives (A,B,A,B,C), forcing c5=A,c8=B,c9=C, so vertex 10 sees all three.
14. [JUSTIFIED] Hence H has no proper 3-coloring, because every possible coloring of its induced 5-cycle leads to a contradiction.
15. [JUSTIFIED] H is triangle-free, has maximum degree 4, and is not 3-colorable; it is therefore a counterexample, so the statement is false.
